title: Registration and device-enrollment data can be linked to a specific household profile
description: During account registration and enrollment of cameras/sensors, the Home Hub receives identifiers such as account details, device serial numbers, network identifiers, and household context in one transaction. If these are combined, the system can link multiple devices and actions to the same homeowner/household, enabling construction of a persistent profile of the home environment.
assumptions: The registration/enrollment flow includes stable identifiers for the user account and enrolled devices.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only provided threat-type applicability, not detailed flow-specific tree nodes.

title: Enrollment messages may identify the homeowner or household
description: Account registration and device enrollment likely contain directly identifying data such as name, email, phone number, address, account username, or uniquely identifying device metadata. If exposed or unnecessarily propagated within the Home Hub, these data can identify the homeowner or their residence.
assumptions: Personally identifying account attributes or uniquely identifying device metadata are transmitted in this flow.
uncertainty_note: Exact identifying fields are not listed in the flow description, but they are typical for account registration and device enrollment.

title: Enrollment data may disclose sensitive details about the home's layout and monitoring setup
description: The set of cameras and sensors being enrolled can reveal private facts about the household, such as which rooms are monitored, whether entry points are instrumented, occupancy/security habits, and the presence of specific smart-home capabilities. This goes beyond simple identification and discloses sensitive characteristics of the home and its occupants.
assumptions: Device types, names, locations, or capabilities are included or inferable during enrollment.
uncertainty_note: Inference depends on how much device metadata is included in the enrollment payload.

title: Registration and enrollment may exceed data minimization
description: The Home Hub may collect more personal data than necessary to create an account and pair devices, such as precise address details, unnecessary profile attributes, persistent device identifiers, or detailed device metadata not required for initial setup. Excessive collection increases privacy risk at the point of ingestion.
assumptions: The implementation may request optional or non-essential personal/device attributes during setup.
uncertainty_note: This is a common setup-flow risk, but the exact fields collected are not specified.

title: The homeowner may be insufficiently informed about what personal and device data are collected during setup
description: If the registration and enrollment interface does not clearly explain what account data, device identifiers, telemetry, and inferred household information are collected and for what purposes, the homeowner cannot form an accurate understanding of the privacy impact of setup.
assumptions: Privacy notices or just-in-time explanations may be absent, incomplete, or hard to understand during onboarding.
uncertainty_note: Applies if transparency is weak in the setup UX; the flow description alone does not confirm the presence or absence of notices.

title: Account registration and device enrollment may occur without valid or sufficiently specific consent/legal basis
description: The setup flow may bundle necessary account creation with optional collection or secondary uses of personal and device data, such as analytics, profiling, or retention of detailed device metadata, without obtaining freely given and specific consent or another appropriate legal basis. This creates a risk of non-compliance with privacy obligations.
assumptions: Some collected data or downstream uses are optional or secondary rather than strictly necessary for service provision.
uncertainty_note: Legal-basis applicability depends on jurisdiction and actual processing purposes; this threat is included because onboarding flows commonly mix necessary and optional processing.

title: Temporary access code can reveal guest identity or visit pattern
description: The Home Hub receives a temporary access code from the guest. If the code is unique per guest or per visit, the hub can infer or record which guest is present and when they attempted entry, exposing identity-related information beyond the immediate unlocking purpose.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are uniquely assigned to a guest, household member, or visit window and that the hub logs or can correlate code submissions.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include specific identifiability node details.

title: Entry code submission discloses presence and access event timing
description: Submitting the temporary access code to the Home Hub discloses personal data about the guest's presence at the property and the time of an attempted or successful entry. This creates a privacy risk if such event data is exposed, retained, or used for secondary purposes.
assumptions: Assumes the hub processes, stores, or transmits access-attempt metadata such as timestamps and success/failure outcomes.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure subtree node is approximate due to missing detailed threat-tree context.

title: Guest may be unaware they are sharing personal data when entering the code
description: A guest entering a temporary access code may not realize that the action shares personal data with the Home Hub, such as the fact of their visit, the time of arrival, and possibly a code linked to their identity or invitation. Lack of notice at the point of entry creates an unawareness risk.
assumptions: Assumes the guest is not clearly informed about what data is collected, how long it is retained, or who can access it.

title: Guest code processing may occur without a valid legal basis or adequate consent/notice
description: Processing the temporary access code and associated access-event metadata may be non-compliant if the household or service provider lacks an appropriate legal basis, fails to provide required privacy information, or retains the data longer than necessary.
assumptions: Assumes applicable privacy regulation or policy governs processing of guest access data and that the hub or associated service stores or otherwise processes this information.
uncertainty_note: Specific non-compliance subtree node is best-judgement because no detailed Nc nodes were provided in the retrieved context.

title: Excessive retention/disclosure of in-home activity history in local event log
description: The Home Hub writes motion, door, and other sensor events into the Local Event Log. These events can reveal occupants' presence, routines, sleep/away patterns, and household behavior. If the log stores more detail, frequency, or retention duration than strictly necessary for local operation, the datastore creates an avoidable disclosure of personal data through accumulated historical records.
assumptions: Sensor events are linked to a household/device context and retained for troubleshooting, automation, or audit purposes beyond immediate transient processing.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgement based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality concepts; retrieved context did not provide the exact subtree node.

title: Identifiability of residents from logged sensor-event patterns
description: Even if the log does not contain explicit names, sequences of motion, door, and sensor events in a home setting can single out a household or specific resident by their distinctive routines and occupancy patterns. Storing fine-grained timestamps and event types in the Local Event Log therefore risks making individuals identifiable from the recorded data.
assumptions: Event timestamps are sufficiently granular and the home environment has a small number of occupants, making behavioral patterns distinctive.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate; identifiability clearly applies, but the retrieved context did not include the relevant subtree.

title: Linkability of separate household activities through a unified event log
description: By writing motion, door, and multiple sensor events into one Local Event Log, the system enables correlation of events across rooms, devices, and times. This can link otherwise separate actions into a coherent activity trail, allowing inference of routines, co-occurrence, and relationships between events that users may not expect to be connected.
assumptions: The datastore aggregates events from multiple sensors/devices under common timestamps, device identifiers, or household identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is best-judgement; threat applicability is strong for aggregated event logs.

title: Detectability of occupancy and behavior from presence of logged events
description: The existence, timing, and volume of entries in the Local Event Log can make private states detectable, such as whether someone is home, asleep, active, or away. Even without reading full payload contents, observing that events are being written at certain times may reveal sensitive household conditions.
assumptions: An observer or component can determine that log writes occur or inspect metadata such as timestamps, counts, or file growth.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; detectability is inferred from event-write metadata rather than explicit content access.

title: Logging of household sensor events without clear necessity or consent basis
description: Persistently writing detailed motion, door, and sensor events to a Local Event Log may exceed what users reasonably expect for core home-hub functionality. If this storage is not transparently justified, configurable, or limited to a lawful/consented purpose, the flow creates a non-compliance risk with data minimization, purpose limitation, transparency, and storage-limitation principles.
assumptions: The system stores these events by default and users may not have granular notice or control over logging scope and retention.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the non-compliance subtree; applicability depends on actual notice, controls, and retention policy.

title: Exposure of highly sensitive video content during upload
description: Recorded camera clips uploaded from the Home Hub to cloud storage may contain intimate in-home activities, occupants, visitors, routines, and other special-category or highly sensitive personal data. If the upload path or handling around the transfer is insufficiently protected, the flow can disclose sensitive personal information to unauthorized parties.
assumptions: Assumes the clips contain identifiable people or household activities and that protection of the transfer path or endpoints may be inadequate.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement from LINDDUN disclosure categories; the retrieved context did not provide the exact D-subtree node for sensitive-content disclosure.

title: Cloud-stored clips enable identification of residents and visitors
description: The uploaded video clips can directly identify data subjects through faces, voices, distinctive clothing, home interiors, timestamps, and contextual cues. Sending these clips to cloud storage increases the chance that individuals captured by the camera can be identified by the cloud provider or anyone gaining access to the stored data.
assumptions: Assumes clips contain visible or inferable identifiers and are accessible to cloud-side personnel, processors, or attackers if controls fail.
uncertainty_note: Exact I-subtree node id is inferred from general LINDDUN identifiability threats because the retrieved context only confirmed applicability at Process->DataStore level.

title: Uploads can be linked to a specific household over time
description: Repeated uploads of camera clips from the same Home Hub to the same cloud video store can be linked together, allowing the cloud service to build a longitudinal profile of one household's occupancy patterns, routines, visitors, and events. Even if individual clips are viewed separately, shared device, account, network, or metadata can link them.
assumptions: Assumes the cloud service can associate uploads via account identifiers, device identifiers, IP addresses, or persistent metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact L-subtree node id is best-effort; the knowledge snippet did not include the detailed linkability tree.

title: Violation of storage limitation for uploaded camera clips
description: Cloud video storage may retain uploaded camera clips longer than necessary for the stated purpose, contrary to the storage limitation principle. Because this flow transfers recorded footage into persistent cloud storage, it creates a concrete risk that personal data about residents, visitors, and bystanders is kept indefinitely or beyond configured retention periods.
assumptions: Assumes retention limits are absent, misconfigured, not enforced, or overridden for backups/logs.

title: Secondary use of uploaded clips beyond home-security purpose
description: Once clips are stored in the cloud, they may be used for purposes beyond the user's expected home-security function, such as analytics, model training, employee review, law-enforcement sharing, or product improvement. This creates a privacy threat that the data is processed in ways unforeseen by the data subjects captured in the footage.
assumptions: Assumes the provider's governance, contracts, or technical controls do not strictly limit downstream use of stored clips.
uncertainty_note: Exact U-subtree node id is inferred from generic unawareness/secondary-use threats; retrieved context did not include the detailed U tree.

title: Insufficient evidence about who uploaded which clip and under what authority
description: If the upload flow does not create reliable, privacy-respecting records of consent, configuration, and upload actions, the system may be unable to demonstrate whether a clip was uploaded legitimately, whether recording/upload was enabled by the user, or whether a disputed upload occurred. This can undermine accountability for privacy-relevant actions affecting captured individuals.
assumptions: Assumes disputes may arise about whether recording or cloud upload was enabled and that audit evidence is incomplete or unreliable.
uncertainty_note: Applicability is moderate rather than certain because repudiation threats depend on the presence or absence of audit/accountability mechanisms not described in the flow.

title: Excessive disclosure of occupancy information in motion alerts
description: The Home Hub may forward more personal data than necessary in a real-time motion alert to the backend, such as precise timestamps, room/device identifiers, continuous event streams, or contextual metadata that reveal household presence and behavior patterns. This creates avoidable disclosure because occupancy-related data is highly privacy-sensitive and only the minimum data needed to deliver the alert should be sent.
assumptions: The motion alert contains personal or household behavioral data and crosses a trust boundary from the home environment to backend infrastructure.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is best-judgement based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality concepts; the retrieved context did not provide the exact Dd subtree.

title: Linkability of repeated motion alerts to the same household or user
description: If the backend receives persistent hub identifiers, account identifiers, stable device IDs, or consistent metadata with each motion alert, it can link multiple alerts over time to the same household. This enables reconstruction of routines, occupancy schedules, and activity patterns beyond what is necessary for handling a single alert.
assumptions: Alerts include stable identifiers or metadata that allow correlation across events at the backend.
uncertainty_note: Exact L subtree node id is inferred from standard LINDDUN linkability patterns; confirm against the project's canonical threat tree.

title: Backend can identify the household behind a motion event
description: A motion alert may be directly or indirectly attributable to a specific household or resident when combined with account data, network identifiers, installation records, or device registration information at the backend. This turns a behavioral event into identified personal data.
assumptions: The backend has access to subscriber, installation, or account records that can associate the incoming alert with a natural person or household.
uncertainty_note: Exact I subtree node id is best-judgement; retrieved context only established applicability of Identifiability to Process->Process flows.

title: Inference of sensitive household behavior from motion-alert patterns
description: Even if each alert appears limited, the backend can derive sensitive information from timing and frequency of motion alerts, such as when occupants are home, asleep, away, or following regular routines. Such detectability of private activities from event patterns can expose sensitive behavioral information.
assumptions: The backend stores or observes alert timing/frequency and can analyze patterns over time.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine inference/detectability concern for event telemetry, but the exact D node id should be validated against the canonical LINDDUN Pro tree.

title: Motion alerts may be processed for secondary purposes without adequate transparency or consent basis
description: Once motion alerts reach the backend, they may be reused for analytics, service improvement, profiling, or retention beyond immediate notification delivery. If users have not been clearly informed or have not consented where required, the flow creates a non-compliance risk with purpose limitation, transparency, and data minimization obligations.
assumptions: The backend may retain or repurpose incoming alert data beyond the strictly necessary operational purpose.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on actual notices, legal basis, and retention practices, which are not provided here.

title: Excessive notification content discloses personal data on the phone lock screen
description: The backend may include more personal data than necessary in the motion-detected push notification (e.g., exact time, camera/location identifier, image preview, occupancy implications). Because push notifications are transferred to and displayed by the homeowner's device, this can disclose personal data to anyone with incidental access to the screen or notification channel. The privacy issue is avoidable if the notification is minimized to only what is necessary.
assumptions: Assumes the push notification can contain detailed event metadata or media preview rather than a generic alert.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement based on LINDDUN Pro disclosure/minimization concepts; retrieved context confirms Dd applies to Process->ExternalEntity flows but does not provide the exact subtree node.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of notification-triggered personal-data sharing
description: The backend sends motion-event information to the homeowner's phone, but the user may not be sufficiently informed about what exact data is included in notifications, when notifications are sent, and under which device/privacy settings content may be visible on the lock screen or through third-party push services. This creates a lack of transparency about processing and disclosure associated with the notification flow.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly explain notification contents, delivery path, and visibility implications.
uncertainty_note: Exact U subtree node is inferred from general unawareness/transparency patterns; retrieved context only establishes that U is applicable on this flow type.

title: Notification delivery and content may exceed the homeowner's consent or preferences
description: If the backend pushes motion-detected notifications without respecting the homeowner's configured preferences or consent choices (e.g., disabled alerts, quiet hours, limited content, selected cameras only), personal data is processed and disclosed beyond the user's authorized scope. This is a consent/non-compliance risk on the outbound notification flow.
assumptions: Assumes notification preferences or consent choices exist or are expected for this kind of monitoring system.
uncertainty_note: Exact Nc subtree node is best-judgement; context supports Nc applicability for Process->ExternalEntity flows but not the precise node.

title: Shared analytics may remain linkable across datasets or over time
description: Even if the backend shares only aggregated device-usage analytics, the transmitted records may still contain stable dimensions, cohort keys, timestamps, app/version breakdowns, geography, or campaign identifiers that allow the vendor to correlate repeated uploads or combine them with other customer data. This can let the vendor link observations about the same user segment, device population, or potentially individual users if aggregation is weak.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics payload includes persistent or quasi-identifying dimensions, fine-grained timestamps, or small-cell aggregates rather than strongly anonymized statistics.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types by interaction/position but not the detailed subtree for this specific case.

title: Vendor may infer identities or single out users from insufficiently aggregated analytics
description: The cloud analytics vendor receives the analytics and may be able to identify a person or device indirectly if aggregates are too granular, if rare combinations are present, or if the vendor can combine the data with other information it already holds. Small cohorts, unique usage patterns, or detailed segmentation can undermine the intended aggregation.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation thresholds, suppression, or k-anonymity-style controls are absent or weak, and that the vendor has auxiliary data available.
uncertainty_note: Applies if the 'aggregated' analytics are not robustly anonymized; if only high-level statistics are shared, this threat may be low or not applicable.

title: Analytics reveal behavioral patterns about users or groups
description: Device-usage analytics can disclose sensitive behavioral information such as feature adoption, session timing, engagement intensity, location-related patterns, or inferred interests. At the vendor, these analytics may reveal private facts about users or small groups even without explicit identifiers.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics include dimensions from which behavior, habits, or sensitive app usage patterns can be inferred.
uncertainty_note: This depends on the semantic richness and granularity of the analytics payload.

title: Sharing analytics with a third-party vendor may exceed users' expectations
description: Users may not expect their app-usage data to be disclosed to an external analytics vendor, especially if the transfer is not clearly communicated or if the vendor uses the data for broader analytics, benchmarking, or service improvement. The disclosure itself can therefore create a privacy threat.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor is a separate controller or processor outside the user's immediate expectation boundary and that disclosure notices are limited or unclear.
uncertainty_note: If the vendor relationship and disclosure are prominently explained and contractually limited, the risk is reduced.

title: Secondary use by the analytics vendor may be unclear or uncontrollable
description: Once the backend sends analytics to the cloud vendor, users may lack visibility into how long the vendor retains the data, whether it is combined with other datasets, and whether it is used for product improvement, benchmarking, model training, or other secondary purposes. This creates unawareness about downstream processing.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor's downstream processing, retention, and sharing practices are not fully transparent to users.
uncertainty_note: Best-judgement tree node; exact subtree may differ depending on the LINDDUN Pro catalog version.

title: Transfer of analytics to the vendor may lack a valid privacy basis or exceed declared purpose
description: Sending device-usage analytics to an external vendor can violate privacy requirements if the transfer is not covered by the app's notice, consent, contract, legitimate-interest assessment, data-processing agreement, cross-border transfer mechanism, or data-minimization commitments. Aggregation alone does not guarantee compliance if the data remains personal or re-identifiable.
assumptions: Assumes applicable legal or policy obligations require transparency, purpose limitation, minimization, and appropriate third-party safeguards.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends heavily on jurisdiction, contractual setup, and whether the shared analytics qualify as anonymous or personal data.

title: Backend retrieval of stored video can reveal viewing patterns and household activity
description: When P2 retrieves a stored video clip from DS2 for playback, the retrieval event itself can expose that a specific homeowner is accessing footage at a particular time. Correlating clip identifiers, account context, timestamps, and camera metadata may allow linking the request to a household, routines, occupancy, or incidents captured in the video.
assumptions: P2 can associate the retrieval with a user account, device session, camera, or clip metadata, and logs or internal telemetry retain this context.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types by interaction/position but not the detailed LINDDUN Pro subtree for this exact case.

title: Backend can identify the homeowner through clip retrieval context
description: The retrieval request handled by P2 may contain or be joined with identifiers such as account ID, device token, camera ID, subscription details, or network/session metadata. This can make the homeowner directly or indirectly identifiable when requesting playback of a stored clip.
assumptions: P2 has access to account/session identifiers or can combine retrieval metadata with existing customer records.
uncertainty_note: Detailed subtree citation is approximate; applicability of identifiability is strong for authenticated playback flows.

title: Playback retrieval may disclose personal video content beyond what is necessary
description: P2 receives the stored video clip and may process or expose more personal data than needed for playback, such as full-resolution footage, extended time ranges, embedded metadata, audio tracks, or clips containing bystanders and neighbors. This increases the risk of unnecessary disclosure of personal data during retrieval.
assumptions: The backend retrieves full objects or rich metadata from storage rather than a minimized subset strictly necessary for the requested playback.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; the threat is grounded in excessive disclosure/minimization concerns at the receiving process.

title: Backend retrieval can expose sensitive inferences from video content
description: By retrieving and handling stored clips, P2 may access footage from which sensitive information can be derived, such as presence at home, daily routines, visitors, children, health-related situations, religious practices, or security incidents. Even if the purpose is playback, the retrieval enables access to data from which such sensitive attributes may be detected or inferred.
assumptions: Stored clips may contain scenes or metadata from which special-category or otherwise sensitive personal information can be inferred.
uncertainty_note: Subtree id is best-effort; the sensitive-data-disclosure risk clearly applies, but the exact node may vary by the project’s threat-tree version.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of backend-side processing during video retrieval
description: The homeowner may expect simple playback, while P2 may also log retrieval events, inspect metadata, generate analytics, cache clips, or use the access event for operational or product purposes. If these backend-side actions are not transparent, the data subject may lack awareness of how their video and viewing activity are processed during retrieval.
assumptions: The service performs backend logging, caching, analytics, or other secondary processing associated with clip retrieval.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; lack of transparency/unawareness is the core concern.

title: Retrieval processing may be incompatible with the original purpose of storing the clip
description: P2 may use the retrieved clip or associated access metadata for purposes beyond homeowner playback, such as service analytics, model training, employee troubleshooting, fraud profiling, or retention in caches/logs. If such processing is not compatible with the original purpose and legal basis communicated to the user, this creates a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Retrieved clips or retrieval metadata are reused beyond immediate playback delivery, or retained longer than necessary.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on the actual stated purposes, legal basis, and retention practices, which are not provided here.
